activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: Stress can show up in the body as headaches, a tight or upset stomach, sweaty palms or trouble falling asleep.
story:
Sawyer had been at his grandfather's house for three Sunday nights in a row, since his parents were away, and every single one had ended the same way: him lying in the guest room with his stomach churning like a washing machine, wide awake until nearly midnight. Sunday night number four was starting the same. His palms were damp, a headache was creeping in behind his eyes, and he could not fall asleep even though he was exhausted.

He sat up and turned on the lamp. There had to be a reason. He got out the small notebook his grandfather kept by the phone and started writing things down, because Grandpa always said that if you wanted to clarify a problem, you put it on paper where you could look at it. Sawyer wrote: Sunday night. Stomach upset. Sweaty palms. Headache. Couldn't sleep. Then he wrote the other three Sundays. Same list, every time. But on Friday and Saturday nights, he slept fine. So it was not the mattress, and it was not something he ate, because Grandpa made the same aggressive amount of spaghetti every night, Sunday included.

"Something on Mondays?" Grandpa asked from the doorway, holding two glasses of milk. He had knocked once and Sawyer had not heard it.

"I have math first period," Sawyer said slowly. "But I have math every day." He stared at the notebook. Mondays were not the same as every day, though. He flipped back in his memory. Two Mondays ago, Ms. Mendoza had sprung a pop quiz. The Monday before that, he had been called to the board and gotten the problem wrong in front of Megane and the whole class. His stomach had gone tight that morning, too, now that he thought about it. He had blamed the cafeteria pancakes.

"So it's not a microbe or anything," he said, almost to himself. "It's Mondays."

Grandpa handed him the milk and sat on the edge of the bed. "In the war, before a big jump, my hands would sweat so bad I could barely grip the rail. Body knew before I did." He tapped his own chest. "Slow breathing helps. Four counts in, hold, four counts out. I still do it when the news gets loud."

Sawyer was skeptical. Breathing was just breathing. But he lay back, set his phone timer for ten minutes, and tried it anyway, counting in the dark. In, two, three, four. Hold. Out, two, three, four. His stomach unclenched a little, the way a fist does when you stop thinking about the argument that made it. He kept going until the timer buzzed, and after that he was asleep before he could check the clock.

Friday, he told Megane and Caleb about it at lunch, drawing a chart of his four Sundays on a napkin. Megane leaned in and said she got headaches every Sunday night and had never once connected it to her Monday morning band solos. Caleb pulled out his own phone and set a recurring reminder for Sunday, nine p.m., that just said BREATHE.

Sunday night number five, Sawyer did his ten minutes of slow breathing with the lamp off, then set his alarm, put his phone across the room so he would not lie there staring at it, and arranged tomorrow's clothes so the morning would be easy. His stomach stayed quiet. Just after he closed his eyes, his phone lit up across the room with Caleb's name and a single message: "Still awake?"

Sawyer grinned in the dark, pulled the blanket to his chin, and texted back, "Not for long."

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
knowledge_domain: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
fact: In Japan, tipping in restaurants is generally not expected, and leaving extra money on the table can confuse the staff.
story:
Rebecca spread her flashcards across the kitchen table until they looked like a small city in an earthquake. One card said "kore o kudasai," please give me this. Another said "ikura desu ka," how much is it. Tomorrow was her birthday, and she had chosen the new Japanese restaurant three blocks away, the one with the paper lanterns, and she was determined to order her whole meal in Japanese instead of pointing at the menu like a lost tourist. The problem was that the words kept sliding out of her head the way water slides through a sieve.

She called Lilya, who arrived ten minutes later with her backpack still on and a transparent folder full of her own notes from when Lilya's cousin taught her three words of Japanese last summer. "I'll be the server," Lilya announced, standing behind the kitchen counter as if it were a restaurant station. "Irasshaimase. What would you like?"

Rebecca picked up a card, set it down, and made herself look at the counter instead. "Kore o kudasai," she said, pointing at an imaginary menu. Then her mind went blank. The question about price, the one she needed most, had vanished. She tried humming it, writing it, saying it into the refrigerator, and each time it escaped again. Was there a pattern she was missing? She noticed that the phrases she remembered best were the ones she had put into a sentence with a gesture, so she pointed at a real object, the teapot, and asked, "Ikura desu ka?" It stuck, like a stamp pressed into dough.

Just then Frederic called on the tablet, and Rebecca told him about the plan. "Oh, we went to Japan last spring," he said. "Funny thing. My dad left some extra bills on the table after dinner, and the server ran half a block down the street to give the money back. He looked so worried. Turns out in Japan tipping isn't expected at all. Leaving extra money on the table just confuses the staff."

Rebecca sat with that for a second. So her birthday money would go exactly to the bill, not a coin more, and nobody would chase her down the street. She had been ready to oppose that idea when her dad suggested it, because at the diner near school a tip was just what you did, but apparently rules could flip depending on where you were. She decided to lay siege to the phrases one more time, cornering each word until it surrendered.

"Round two," Lilya said from behind the counter, straightening an invisible apron. "Irasshaimase."

"Kore o kudasai," said Rebecca, pointing at the teapot without a single flashcard in sight. "Ikura desu ka?"

activity: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
knowledge_domain: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
fact: In French, the simple future is also built on the infinitive: "parler" (to speak) becomes "je parlerai," meaning "I will speak."
story:
Avery sprawled across Mikayla's kitchen table, her French worksheet curling at the corners. The assignment wanted a paragraph about next year's plans, everything in the future tense, and so far she had written one sentence and crossed out half of it.

"Je vais..." she began, and stopped. She knew how to say she was going to do something, but Ms. Lombardi wanted the real future tense, the kind that changed the verb itself. Athena, across the table, had already filled half a page.

"I keep messing up the endings," Avery said, tapping her pencil. "Je parler, je parle, je parlerai?"

Athena leaned over, and Avery noticed her friend was smiling in a strange way, like she was holding a secret. "You take Spanish too, right? Look at your Spanish notes."

Avery dug through her binder until she found the Spanish page from last semester. Hablar became hablaré. Speak became will speak. Then she looked back at the French: parler became parlerai. The two sat side by side on the table, and something clicked, quiet and sudden, like a light coming on in a room she hadn't known was dark. The French future was built on the infinitive, just the way Spanish did it. Parler, to speak, plus an ending, and you got je parlerai, I will speak. The languages ran parallel to each other, two roads heading the same direction.

She tested it at once, propelling her pencil across the paper. Finir, to finish. Je finirai, I will finish. Visiter, to visit. Je visiterai, I will visit. She checked Athena's page, and there it was in Athena's neat handwriting, the same pattern again and again.

"Wait," Mikayla said, wandering in with a bag of chips. "How did you figure that out without the textbook?"

"I used my Spanish notes," Avery said. "It's almost the same trick."

For the next twenty minutes the paragraph grew sentence by sentence. Je visiterai ma grand-mère. J'apprendrai la natation. When Avery got an ending wrong, she went back to her Spanish notes, found the matching verb, and fixed it herself. Athena read the finished paragraph out loud once, and Avery copied the last line for a citation at the bottom, the page number from the workbook that Ms. Lombardi always demanded.

On Monday, Ms. Lombardi returned the papers. Avery flipped hers over and saw the grade circled at the top, high and clean. Then she read the comment in the margin: "Excellent work. Next time, try writing it without leaning on your Spanish."

Avery laughed. "But the Spanish is what got me the grade."

Ms. Lombardi handed back Athena's paper next. At the bottom, in Athena's citation, was the Spanish workbook's page number.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: In 2009, scientists led by Aniruddh Patel showed that Snowball, a sulphur-crested cockatoo, could move in time to music and adjust when the tempo changed.
story:
Simon stood at the edge of the school parking lot, where the streetlight made a pale circle on the asphalt, and told himself that walking through the gym doors was a separate problem from standing here. The dance had started twenty minutes ago. Through the brick he could hear the bass thumping, and he could see, through the propped door, Leandre and Jan already out on the floor with the crowd of eighth graders.

His problem was not the walking. His problem was that he could not dance, and he had no way to practice without being seen, which meant he could not fix the problem before it became public. He turned this over while a car pulled out of the far row and its headlights swept across the painted lines.

Then he remembered the video Leandre had shown him last week in the computer lab. A white cockatoo named Snowball, bopping its crested head while a song played. "In 2009," Leandre had said, reading off the screen, "scientists led by Aniruddh Patel showed Snowball could move in time to music and adjust when the tempo changed." A bird. Keeping the beat. If a cockatoo could do that, Simon reasoned, then keeping a beat was not some talent you were born with or without; it was something a creature could just do if it paid attention to the sound.

He had a way to test it. He pulled out one earbud, kept the other in, and picked a song he liked. His hypothesis was simple: if he tracked the beat instead of thinking about his arms, his body would follow. He tried it in the shadow past the dumpster, half-moving, watching his sneakers. First attempt, he was off, rushing. Second attempt, he counted the thumps and let the counting shrink until it was just listening. On the third try his weight shifted on the right pulse, and it felt less like a step and more like the music moving through him and out again. He did it four more times to be sure it wasn't one lucky anecdote; the cumulative evidence said the trick held.

Ms. Navarro, who was chaperoning and had stepped out for air, had been watching from near the fence. "You could do that inside, you know," she said. "Nobody's grading you."

"That's exactly the problem," Simon said, but he grinned, and she laughed and held the door.

Inside, the song changed tempo, and he noticed his feet slow down with it, the way Snowball adjusted, and that fact steadied him more than any speech could have. He found Jan by the punch table, and when the next song started, Jan said, "You practice in secret?"

"Bird science," Simon said, and held out a hand toward the floor.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Scientists assign people to groups at random so that differences like age or health are likely to be spread evenly, rather than letting people choose their group.
story:
Claire sat at the kitchen computer with a glass of peach nectar and a homework prompt that refused to be finished. Ms. Watanabe wanted them to explain why a new medicine study gave people numbers instead of letting them choose their group. Claire had read the paragraph three times. Why not just ask the volunteers what they wanted? If somebody felt better after taking the medicine, that was good enough for her grandmother, who recommended cherry juice to everyone at bingo.

She texted Zoey, whose cousin had been in a sleep study the year before. "Your cousin said the app worked, right?" The answer came back fast: "Totally. He slept like a rock. It has to work." One person sleeping well was a story, though, and Ms. Watanabe had written "tested evidence" on the board with such force that a piece of chalk had broken. Claire needed to see the difference for herself before she could write a word about it.

Then Carla called, mid-argument with her brother about whether music helped or ruined studying, and Claire had her experiment. She recruited eight classmates through a group chat, promising nothing but the truth. Four claimed music helped, four were sure it wrecked them, and if she let them pick their own groups, she would learn nothing except what they already believed. So she flipped a coin for each name. Heads meant the quiet room, tails meant headphones, and Darren, the loudest music believer in the grade, got heads and looked betrayed by currency.

"Can't I just switch?" he asked when they gathered in her basement.

"That's the whole point," Claire said. "Scientists assign people to groups at random so that differences like age or health are likely to be spread evenly, rather than letting people choose their group."

"That sounds plausible," Darren admitted, though he said it like a surrender.

The next day they all took the same quiz. The music group averaged 76. The quiet group averaged 79, which was close enough that Claire checked her math twice and then a third time. She messaged Zoey the numbers, and Zoey replied that her cousin still slept like a rock. Claire stared at the screen, took a long sip of nectar, and began to type her assignment. In the last paragraph, she wrote that one cousin and eight coin-flipped classmates were not the same kind of proof at all, and that the coin, boring as it was, had done something no amount of choosing could. She hit print, and the paper slid out warm into her hand.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: In one-point perspective, lines that face you squarely, like window tops and doorframes on a building's front, stay perfectly horizontal or vertical.
story:
Clara spread her sketchbook on the picnic table and set the pencil case where the ants couldn't colonize it, since last week they had swarmed a whole cookie in under ten minutes. Griffin dropped onto the bench across from her, chewing a granola bar.

"Show me the street," he said. "Mr. Whitaker's assignment. One-point perspective, lines going to a vanishing point."

Clara turned the pad around. She had drawn a straight road shrinking to a dot in the middle, with shops on both sides and every edge running toward that dot. She had even slanted the tops of the doorframes and the window ledges, making each line lean inward.

Griffin frowned. "The fronts of the shops look like they're tipping over. Like they're all falling into the street."

"They are not." Clara pulled the pad back. "Everything goes to the vanishing point. That's the whole rule."

"Then why do they look wrong?"

Clara stared at the buildings. The walls facing her looked tilted, as if a giant had pushed them. She tried to think of a way to check, and her eyes went past the fence to Mr. Whitaker's house, the flat front of it squarely aimed at her backyard. She grabbed her ruler, held it up at arm's length, and lined it up with the top edge of his kitchen window.

"Griffin, look. Tell me what you see."

He leaned in, crumbs on his chin. "It's flat. The window top goes straight across."

She moved the ruler to the doorframe. Straight up and down. She checked the second-floor windows too, and every line sat level or plumb, not one of them slanting. She lowered the ruler slowly.

"So the lines that run away from me, the sidewalk edges, the rooflines going back, those slant toward the vanishing point. But the ones facing me squarely, like window tops and doorframes on a building's front, they stay horizontal or vertical." She picked up her eraser. "I made every single line slant. That's my mistake."

"That's a legitimate disaster," Griffin said. "Half your eraser's going to die."

She erased the leaning shop fronts and redrew them, ruling crisp horizontal lines for the tops of the windows and vertical lines for the doorframes, letting only the receding edges run toward the dot. When she held the pad up beside the real view of Mr. Whitaker's house, the two matched.

"It looks like an actual street now," Griffin said. "That was a good inference, holding up the ruler like that."

Over the fence, Mr. Whitacker was watering his tomatoes. "That drawing's coming along," he called.

Clara turned the page toward him. "The windows finally stopped falling over."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Historians still do not know who fired the first shot at Lexington in April 1775; British and colonial witnesses each said the other side fired first.
story:
Riley spread the two photocopies across Odin's kitchen table, weighting the corners with salt shakers. The assignment from history club was due Monday, and Ms. Diallo had given each of them a packet: two eyewitness accounts of the same April morning in 1775 at Lexington, one from a British soldier, one from a colonial militiaman. Riley had read both twice on the bus, and something about them made the back of his neck itch.

"Here's the problem," he said when Odin slid into the chair opposite him. "The British guy says the colonists fired first. The colonial guy says the British fired first. Same morning, same green, and they flat-out contradict each other. So one of them is lying, right?"

Odin's little sister was doing cartwheels in the hallway, agile as anything, thumping her feet against the wall until their mother called for quiet from another room. Odin tapped the papers. "Maybe the militiaman wanted to look innocent. Or the soldier did."

"Okay, but here's what's bugging me." Riley flipped to the last page, where Ms. Diallo had typed a note in the margin. He read it out loud: "Historians still do not know who fired the first shot at Lexington in April 1775. British and colonial witnesses each said the other side fired first." He set the paper down. "Nobody knows. Not even now. People have been arguing about it for two hundred and fifty years."

"So the assignment's impossible," Odin said. "Great."

Riley got up and paced the length of the kitchen, which generated a squeak from the floorboard near the sink every time he crossed it. He stopped. He crossed again. Squeak. He crossed faster, and this time there was no sound at all. "Wait. Did you hear that? The floor squeaks when I walk slow but not when I walk fast. If you were in the next room and only heard the squeak, you'd swear I was walking slow. You'd be wrong, but you wouldn't be lying."

Odin frowned. "That's your floor. That's not Lexington."

"But it's the same idea." Riley pulled his notebook over and started sketching the green, the British line, the militia line, the stone walls and buildings around them. "Two guys standing in different spots, smoke everywhere, a shot ringing out, everybody screaming. Each one sees the flash or hears the crack from where he's standing. Maybe both of them honestly believe the other side fired first. Maybe nobody's lying at all."

They spent the next hour marking sight lines on the sketch, and when Yani arrived from her grandmother's residence down the block, she added the best idea yet: they would act it out in the backyard, three kids in two lines, and see what each witness could actually see from position. Riley stood in the militia line, Odin in the British line, and Yani fired the "first shot" by clapping two pie tins together behind the fence.

Afterward they compared notes. Riley had been certain the sound came from the British line. Odin had been certain it came from the militia. Yani held up the pie tins and grinned. "Neither of you. It was me."

"So that's our project," Riley said, already writing the title. "Nobody at Lexington was necessarily lying. Some things just can't be settled."

"It's like the floorboard," Odin said. "Squeak."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Airliner cabins are pressurized, but under regulations the cabin air pressure may be as low as it would be at 8,000 feet (about 2,400 meters) above sea level.
story:
The ferry horn blared, and Charlie sprinted up the ramp with her backpack thumping, because today was the day everything began: a plane ride, a ferry crossing, and a whole week on the island where her grandmother lived. She wedged into a spot at the rail between Carter and Emanuel, who were already arguing about who had seen the first seagull.

"Check this out," Emanuel said, pulling a flattened bag of chips from his jacket. "I bought these in the airport, and on the plane the bag was so fat it looked like a pillow. Now look at it. Sad and wrinkly." He held it up like evidence in a trial. Carter said somebody must have squished it under the seat. Charlie wasn't so sure, because she remembered her own unopened bag of pretzels doing the exact same thing, and nobody had stepped on those.

She flashed back to the plane, three hours ago. The pretzel bag in the seat pocket had been puffed up tight as a balloon, and she had poked it twice and watched it spring back. Her dad had said something quick about the air in the cabin, but he had been halfway asleep, and she had filed the mystery away. Now, on the ferry, she had a theory, and theories needed testing. "Okay," she said. "The bag was fat in the plane and flat everywhere else. So it's not the chips. It's the air up there. The cabin must have less air pressing on it than the air down here, like the cabin is way higher than it feels."

"How high?" Carter asked.

"Mr. Ma said it in science," Emanuel said. "Regulations let the cabin air pressure go as low as it would be at 8,000 feet, about 2,400 meters above sea level."

"That's like flying while sitting on a mountain," Charlie said. To test it, she pulled out the sealed granola bar she had saved from the plane, still looking slightly bloated, and pressed it gently with her thumb. It gave, like a tiny cushion. "See? Still puffy. It'll flatten by tonight, down here at sea level." She wrote it all in her notebook like a lab report, then added a note about her lunch: eat the sandwich today, because a week-old sandwich would start to decompose, and nobody wanted a backpack full of regret.

Her phone buzzed. A message from Carter, standing two feet away, because that was funnier: "IF THE BAG PUFFS UP ON THE WAY HOME CAN WE SIGN IT AND KEEP IT AS A PERMANENT SOUVENIR." Charlie laughed so hard the manatee poster behind her rattled, the one advertising island tours that called the manatee a gentle herbivore that grazed on river grass. She typed back, "Only if you carry it."

The ferry pitched over a wake, spray arced up, and Charlie grabbed the rail with both hands, her notebook flapping. Emanuel shouted that the first one to spot a dolphin got the window seat at Grandmother's house. All three of them leaned out over the water, squinting into the glare, and Charlie pointed and yelled, "There! Right there!"

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: In the United States, a permanent change of address filed with the Postal Service forwards First-Class Mail to the new address for 12 months.
story:
The last box was taped shut when Michael found the envelope on his desk, addressed to Kathryn but never mailed. He had written it two weeks ago, back when the move still felt far away, and now the moving truck was coming tomorrow. He ran downstairs to apartment 2B, where Ms. Grant was sorting mail at the little bank of brass boxes by the lobby door.

"Ms. Grant, if I mail a letter after we leave, will it follow us?"

She tilted her head. "Depends what you mean by follow."

He explained about the form his dad had filled out online, the change of address. Ms. Grant nodded slowly. "Permanent change of address, filed with the Postal Service. First-Class Mail gets forwarded to the new address for twelve months."

Twelve months. Michael said it out loud twice, testing the shape of it. That meant Kathryn could write him in June and the letter would still find the new house, even in March. He sprinted back upstairs, grabbed a stamp from the junk drawer, and raced to the corner mailbox before the last pickup, dropping his letter in with a clang like a bell.

Two hundred miles and one week later, the new apartment smelled like cardboard and floor polish. The stairs were being redone, and a workman had taped a sign about corrosive chemicals near the treads, so Michael took the elevator up with his box of science stuff, including the bean seeds he'd planted in paper cups. If he watered them on the windowsill here, maybe they'd germinate before school started, and he'd have something alive to show for the new place.

On day nine, the mail slot clacked. Michael was closest, so he grabbed the stack, and there it was: Kathryn's looping handwriting, her old street address crossed out with one neat line, the new one printed below. Underneath, in tiny letters, she had written, "Told you the beans would sprout first. Race you."

Michael laughed so loudly that a neighbor leaned out a doorway to see what was happening. He held the envelope up like a trophy, then flipped it over. On the back, Kathryn had drawn a map with an X on it. "Scavenger hunt," it read. "First clue is already on its way."

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Apps must ask permission to use a phone's camera, microphone or contacts, and you can take that permission away later in the phone's settings.
story:
The box sat on the kitchen table between Liam's elbows, and for a full minute he just looked at it. His mother had said it was his, all his, a real phone at last, and she'd left for her shift before he could argue that he didn't need one. He peeled the tape, turned the phone on, and was still picking a wallpaper when Yosef and Anna-Eve banged through the back door, having spotted the glow from the front window across the median that divided their street.

"Download everything," Yosef said immediately, dropping into the chair beside him. "Start with the flashlight. You'll need it for the basement."

Anna-Eve leaned over Liam's other shoulder as he typed in the search. The flashlight app came up first, with a million downloads and a picture of a torch. He tapped install, and then the phone asked him a question. The app wanted permission to use his contacts. All of them. Every name, every number his mother had put in, including her work line and the neighbor Mr. Sun's.

"Why would a flashlight need my contacts?" Liam said.

"It's just what apps do," Yosef said. "Click allow. That's what my brother does."

Liam's thumb hovered, but he didn't tap it. A flashlight only needed the light, he reasoned, and if it wanted more than that, it wanted it for some reason he couldn't see. "Hold on," he said. He tapped deny instead, and the app installed anyway and lit up the whole kitchen with a harsh white beam when he opened it. It worked fine. Better than fine.

"That's not fair to the app," Yosef said.

"It's a flashlight," Anna-Eve said. "It's not your friend." She took the phone and started digging through the settings while Liam ate the last two crackers she'd brought, and she found a screen with a list. Camera, microphone, contacts. Next to each one was a switch, and beside contacts, for a different app Yosef had already sneaked onto the phone while Liam was getting juice, the switch was flipped to on. Anna-Eve flipped it off. "You can take permission away later, right here," she said. "You're not stuck with what you clicked."

Yosef slumped a little. "I only added that game because you were taking so long with your crackers."

Liam looked at the bright screen in his hand, then out the window at the streetlamp above the median, steady and orange and asking nothing from anyone. He set the phone face down on the table. "One app tonight," he said. "And I'm going to bed before ten, phone downstairs, because I know myself."

"That's so boring," Yosef said.

"That's the deal," said Liam, and carried it down the hall.

activity: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
knowledge_domain: to order a meal in a restaurant in a new language and ask how much it costs
fact: In France and many other European countries, prices use a comma where English uses a decimal point, so twelve euros fifty is written "12,50 €."
story:
Leah spread the French menu across the library table and glared at it like it had insulted her grandmother. "Jannah, this sandwich costs one thousand two hundred and fifty euros."

Jannah leaned over, chewing her pen. "Then it had better come with the whole cow."

"I'm serious. Look. Croque-monsieur, 12,50 €. Twelve hundred and fifty. My whole family could go bankrupt on toast." Leah flipped the laminated menu over, hoping the back might be cheaper, but it only listed drinks, and a small orange juice supposedly cost 3,20 €, which was either three hundred and twenty euros or the price of a small house.

Amina arrived with an armful of library books and dropped them beside the French dictionary. "Why are you two buying imaginary sandwiches?"

"Mr. Chowdhury says we have to order lunch in French by Friday," Jannah said. "Speaking part. And Leah has discovered that France is the most expensive country on Earth."

Amina picked up the menu, squinted at it. Her dad ran a shop and she could read a price tag from across a room. "That's not one thousand two hundred and fifty. Think about it. A sandwich for twelve hundred euros? Even at the airport, no."

Leah sat back. There was a pattern here, she was sure of it, like when her granddad insisted the new thermostat was broken until she figured out it was displaying Celsius. She grabbed a pencil and copied the prices into a column: 12,50, then 3,20, then 8,90. Every single one had exactly two digits after the comma. Not one, not three, always two, the way money always has exactly two digits after the decimal point. Her pulse did a small, embarrassing leap. "It's a decimal point. They just write it with a comma instead. So this sandwich is twelve euros fifty, not a thousand anything."

"Prove it," Jannah said, because that was Jannah's job.

Leah carried the menu to the geography shelf and dug out a book on France, the one with the transparent plastic dust jacket that showed the Eiffel Tower underneath. She flipped until she found a photo of a real chalkboard outside a real café. Soupe à l'oignon, 6,80 €. Beside it, a small line of English for tourists: soup, 6.80 euros. Same price, different punctuation. She held the book up like a courtroom exhibit. "In France, and a lot of other European countries, they use a comma where we use a decimal point. Twelve euros fifty is written 12,50 €."

"So my orange juice is three twenty," Amina said, "and you owe me an apology to France."

Leah grinned and pulled the worksheet toward her. Now she could practice for real. "Je voudrais un croque-monsieur," she began, then paused. "How do I ask how much it costs?"

"Combien ça coûte," said Amina, who had been memorizing phrases since Tuesday.

"Combien ça coûte?" Leah tried, and Jannah, holding a ruler like a waiter's tray, replied in an outrageous accent, "Douze euros cinquante, mademoiselle."

"Only twelve fifty," Leah said. "I'll take two. And a pension, in case I need somewhere to sleep off lunch."

"That's a guesthouse, not a nap hotel," Amina said.

"Then I'll install myself in one for the whole summer," Leah said, and slid her coins across the table. "Keep the change, waiter. Buy yourself a comma."

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: In the United States, the Truth in Savings Act of 1991 requires banks to state savings rates as an annual percentage yield, or APY, which includes the effect of compounding.
story:
David taped the last sign to the front of the lemonade stand: five dollars a cup, fund for the new bike. He had forty-two dollars in the coffee can under the register box, and the bike cost two hundred. Jannah counted cups while Raylan stacked ice, and between customers David worked on his math notebook, because Ms. Lawson had assigned them a project: pick a real savings plan, and show what the money would do over five years.

The problem was the poster. The bank three doors down had taped a flyer in its window, and it listed two numbers, an interest rate and then, underneath, a slightly higher number labeled APY. David copied both into his notebook and stared at them on the walk back. Simple interest, he knew, meant the bank paid you the same amount every year, so five years of it made a neat, straight stack. But something about that second number nagged him. Why would the bank bother printing two?

Raylan was no help. "Take the bigger one," he said, wiping lemon pulp off his hands. "Bigger is better. End of story." Jannah texted her older sister, and when the reply came back it said only, "Truth in Savings Act, 1991. Look it up, it's the law." So David looked it up on the library computer during their afternoon break. In the United States, a law called the Truth in Savings Act of 1991 requires banks to state savings rates as an annual percentage yield, or APY, and that APY includes the effect of compounding. He read the line twice. Raylan peered over his shoulder, still stubborn. "Fine, but what's compounding?" David didn't answer yet, because he wanted to see it for himself first.

Back at the stand, he set up the test. He wrote two five-year plans side by side in the notebook. In the first, simple interest paid a flat amount each year, and the total grew in even steps. In the second, he let each year's interest join the balance, so the next year's payment was calculated on a bigger number, and the steps climbed. When he added the fifth year, the compound column finished ahead. He slid the notebook across the table to Raylan and pointed at the flyer's APY. "That's the number that already includes the compounding," David said. "It's the real one."

At closing time, Ms. Lawson stopped by for a cup, quarters ready in her palm. She noticed the notebook open beside the sugar bowl and read the two columns, then the copied poster numbers. "Which one are you choosing for the bike fund?" she asked. David looked at the coffee can, then at the higher figure at the bottom of the compound column, and started doing the arithmetic on the back of a napkin.

"You're going to need a bigger can," Jannah said.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: When a price is kept below the equilibrium price, more people want the item than there are items for sale, and economists call that gap a shortage.
story:
Henry stood in line at the gas station counter, holding the last two energy drinks in the cooler, and behind him the line stretched all the way to the door. The drinks were on sale for a dollar each, half the usual price, and by noon the shelf would be empty again. He knew this because he had been here yesterday at the same time and had watched a man in a delivery uniform sweep the last six cans into his arms.

"Take one," said Dean, who was next in line. "There's like nine people behind us."

Henry looked at the row of people waiting, at the empty shelf behind the clerk, at the handwritten sign that said SALE, $1. He could take both, or he could take one, and something about that choice reminded him of the concert tickets last spring. Mickael had camped on the ticket site at exactly ten in the morning, refreshing the page while Henry watched over his shoulder. The tickets were cheap, forty dollars, and they were gone in under four minutes. Hundreds of fans, Mickael said afterward, got nothing at all. Henry had gotten nothing too, and he remembered standing in Mickael's kitchen afterward, both of them staring at the sold-out screen.

"Hey," Henry said now, turning to Dean. "You know how Mr. Tan calls it a shortage when more people want something than there are of it? That's what happened with those tickets. The price was low, so everybody wanted in, and there just weren't enough."

Dean shrugged. "So charge more and the line goes away?"

"I think so. I mean, look around." Henry pointed at the coffee machine, where there were twenty cups ready and nobody waiting. Coffee cost three dollars. The dollar drinks had a line out the door. He turned back to the counter and set one can down, keeping the other.

"You're testing it," Dean said. "You're leaving one to see if it helps."

"It's one can," Henry said. "It's not going to fix anything." But he watched anyway, while the clerk rang him up, as the guy behind Dean grabbed the last can and the guy after him stared at the bare shelf and swore quietly.

That night Henry found a message from Mickael on his phone. "Did you get a drink? Also, the band added a second show. Tickets are eighty dollars this time. Took two days to sell. Still some left." Henry read it twice. Higher price, longer lines of supply, and nobody shut out in four minutes. He had left one can on that shelf for nothing, probably, and he knew it. He typed back, "Got one. Keeping the receipt for science," and set the phone face down on his desk, next to the useless ticket confirmation from last spring.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Clothes left crumpled in a dryer or basket after the cycle ends tend to wrinkle as they cool, so taking them out promptly and folding them helps keep them smooth.
story:
Stella stood in her grandmother's laundry room holding a red sock above two separate piles, trying to decide whether one sock could really turn a whole load pink. Her grandmother had gone to the garden, so the only guidance came from a taped-up note that said, "Cold for darks, warm for lights, and don't ask the dryer to accommodate your forgetfulness."

The problem was that Stella's older brother had a job interview tomorrow morning, and his one good shirt was crumpled at the bottom of the hamper. Last month, when she'd washed his gym clothes while he was away, she'd left them in the dryer overnight because Flora had texted about a movie, and the shirt had come out looking like a folded paper fan. He'd worn it anyway. Nobody had said much, but Stella had noticed.

She sorted the laundry into darks and lights, checked pockets, and started the shirt in a small load by itself. While the washer ran, Zorawar called from the porch, and she told him her theory. "I think it's not the washing that ruins them. I think it's what happens after." He said that sounded like an inference, which was his word of the week from Mr. Campbell's class, and Stella said it sounded like a plan.

When the dryer buzzed, she was standing next to it, ready. She pulled the shirt out warm and shook it out flat on the counter. It was smooth. Almost completely smooth. She folded it the way her grandmother folded tablecloths, in thirds, and set it on top of the basket like evidence.

Her grandmother came in with dirt on her hands and looked at the folded shirt, then at Stella. "So you figured out why your brother's last one looked like a raisin." Stella admitted the experiment, and that she'd felt bad about the raisin shirt for weeks without saying so. Her grandmother was indifferent to the confession itself, but not to the shirt. "Tomorrow morning he'll look hired," she said, and turned to the sink.

That night Stella checked the dryer one last time before bed, then moved the whole basket into the hall so nobody could forget it. In the morning her brother came downstairs in the smooth shirt, adjusting his collar in the hallway mirror. He stopped, looked at himself, and said, "Did you iron this?" Stella picked up her toast and took a bite.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Results from a large sample are generally more reliable than results from a few people, because chance differences between individuals tend to even out in larger groups.
story:
The waiting room smelled like disinfectant, and James sat between Tobias and a rack of torn magazines, coughing into his elbow. He pulled out his phone and showed Tobias the list he had typed at two in the morning. "Three for three," he said. "Aviraj, you, and me. We all took vitamin C last winter and none of us got a cold. That's a hundred percent."

Tobias scrolled through it without smiling. "My gran took it for forty years and never got one either."

"I know. So it works." James coughed again, harder, and a man across the room glanced over. An old poster on the wall reminded patients to cover coughs and wash hands, and under the word hygiene there was a drawing of two hands under running water. James stared at it because he did not want to look at the clock. Dr. Ferris was running twenty minutes late, and every minute he sat there, his theory felt more solid.

The doctor called him back, listened to his chest, and said it was a virus that could mimic a bad cold in its first days but would clear on its own. On the desk she had left open a medical magazine, and while she wrote his note, James read the page facing him. A study of four hundred adults had tracked vitamin C through an entire cold season. Half took the pills, half took lookalike pills, and the two groups caught colds at almost exactly the same rate. Four hundred people. He read the sentence twice.

He remembered then, the way you remember something you would rather not. Last month Aviraj had run a survey in Mr. Nikolaidis's class about the cafeteria's new chilli, asking two hundred students whether they liked it. The first day, Aviraj had asked only three kids at his lab table and announced that everyone loved it. Then the big survey came back and the chilli scored near the bottom of the menu. Aviraj had shrugged and said, "Three people is not the same as two hundred. Three can all be weird." James had laughed at that. He was not laughing now.

Three friends, one winter, no colds. Two hundred students, a true vote. Four hundred adults, a season of data. He turned the magazine toward Dr. Ferris before he could talk himself out of it. "Does this mean the vitamin C thing doesn't work?"

She glanced at the page. "That's what the big numbers say."

"So Aviraj and me and Tobias, we were just lucky." She nodded and handed him the note for school. He texted Tobias from the hallway: delete the list. Big surveys beat small ones.

Tobias wrote back one word. "Gran?"

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: A voice deepens during puberty because the larynx grows and the vocal folds inside it get longer and thicker, and the voice may crack while this happens.
story:
The cracking had gotten worse all week, and Simon decided the pharmacy would have something for it. He stood in front of the throat aisle, a consumer with a mission, scanning shelves of lozenges, sprays and teas while his best friend Lex trailed behind him, reading labels aloud in a fake radio voice. "Emergency Vocal Repair Kit," Lex announced, holding up a box of honey-lemon drops that promised to dissolve slowly and soothe irritated tissue. Simon took the box. It seemed reasonable. His throat wasn't sore, exactly, but something in there was clearly broken, because every time he sang the solo line in choir, the note split in half like a dropped plate.

"Those are for sore throats," said Adelaide, who had biked over to meet them and was now examining a display of lip balm. "A crack isn't soreness. It's more like a machine problem." Simon rolled the box over in his hands anyway. He wanted the solo at the winter concert, and he wanted it in two weeks, so whatever was wrong needed a fix, fast.

At the counter, Ms. Silva, the pharmacist who lived three doors down from Simon, rang up the drops and studied him for a second. "Voice trouble?" she asked. Simon nodded and described it: fine on the low notes, fine in the morning, and then halfway up a high note the sound just snapped. Ms. Silva didn't reach for another product. "That's not something in the aisles," she said. "It happened to my brother. It's the voice box growing. Ask your choir teacher about the vocal folds." Lex frowned. "Vocal folds?" Ms. Silva tapped her own throat. "That's the exact word," she said. "The larynx grows during puberty, and the vocal folds inside it get longer and thicker, and while that happens the voice can crack." Then she handed over the lozenges anyway, since he'd already paid, and told him the drops would help his throat feel nice even if they couldn't fix the snap.

Simon tested the idea that afternoon in the choir room after school. He sang the solo line quietly, then louder, and felt for the exact spot where the sound split. The crack wasn't random; it lived in a narrow band of notes, parallel to the high range he used to own. Below the band he was fine, and above it he was fine, and his new low notes were deeper than anything he'd managed last year. Longer and thicker, he thought. Like the rest of him had grown, the parts inside had grown too. Adelaide held the pitch on the piano and called out, "Again," each time the note broke, and Simon tried again, riding the break instead of flinching from it.

At the next rehearsal, the choir teacher moved the solo down a few steps, and Simon got through the whole line without a single crack. Adelaide grinned at him from the second row. Lex, in the back, mouthed the words emergency vocal repair kit, and Simon, holding the final low note, felt it land steady and true.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Samuel Johnson's 'A Dictionary of the English Language', published in 1755, helped settle how many English words were spelled.
story:
Kate had found the old dictionary in the library on Tuesday, three days before the spelling bee, when she was supposed to be studying her word lists. It was enormous, with a cracked leather cover, and when she opened it Mr. Farah-Ali, the librarian, leaned over the desk and said, "Samuel Johnson's dictionary. Published in 1755. It helped settle how many English words were spelled." Kate had stared at the faded pages. She had always assumed spellings just existed, the way rivers exist, and it felt bizarre to imagine a person deciding them, one by one, in a room somewhere.

Now she stood on the auditorium stage under the hot lights, with Myla in the second row chewing her thumbnail, and the pronouncer said, "Your word is herbivore." Kate's mind went briefly white. Then she thought about the dictionary, about all those settled spellings, and about a pattern she had noticed while studying: words that came from Latin chunks were often trickier than they sounded, but the tricky part hid in the middle, not the start. Herbivore had to start the way "herb" did. The part she needed to test was the ending. "Could I have the definition?" she asked. "An animal that eats only plants," the pronouncer said. In her head she placed the word beside "carnivore" and "omnivore," which she had spelled correctly in practice last week, and both of those ended the same way. The rule, if it was a rule, would not conceal itself in the last three letters.

"H-E-R-B-I-V-O-R-E," she said. "Herbivore."

The bell of the judge's pencil tapping paper told her she had it, and the small audience in the folding chairs clapped. Two rounds later, the boy beside her, who had been winning everything since fourth grade, sat down after missing "separate," and Kate felt a strange, quiet shift in herself. She had spent the whole week certain she would lose in the first round, certain that spelling was a talent some people simply had. Now she was not so sure. Maybe spelling was more like the old dictionary: a long pile of decisions and patterns that a person could actually work through, if she took the time.

Round five came down to Kate and one other girl, a seventh grader Kate barely knew. The auditorium clock above the exit door said the bee had to end by four o'clock, because the custodian needed to lock the building, and the judges were glancing up at it between words. The pronouncer checked his list and said, "Your word is pavilion."

Kate asked for the language of origin. "French," the pronouncer said, and Kate nodded slowly. French endings were the ones that liked extra letters, the ones that did not sound the way they looked. She remembered the double L she had almost missed in "gorilla's cousin" during practice, and how "millennium" had that double N lurking in the middle. If pavilion was French, the odd letter was probably a second L.

"P-A-V-I-L-L-I-O-N," she said. "Pavilion."

The judges conferred, and then the head judge raised her hand toward Kate and said, "That is correct, and that is the winning word." Myla was already on her feet, and somewhere in the back Mr. Farah-Ali clapped louder than anyone. Kate walked off the stage carrying the small trophy, and when she reached the library table she set it down beside the old dictionary, open to the page it had fallen to earlier, and read the first word at the top of the column.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: A glow stick shines brighter but runs out faster when it is warm, and glows dimmer but lasts longer when it is cold.
story:
Cooper stood in Eloi's kitchen holding three glow sticks that were supposed to last until midnight, and the dance started at seven. Eloi's older sister had bought a whole tube of them on sale last summer, and now Cooper noticed something odd: the two from her car, which had baked on the dashboard all afternoon, were blazing bright, while the one from the cool basement was barely a ghost of green.

"How can the same glow stick be that different?" Cooper asked. He cracked the dim one fresh and set it beside the hot ones on the counter. The bright ones outshone it like flashlights next to a nightlight.

Lilah arrived with her dress in a garment bag and leaned over the counter too. "Maybe the hot ones are just newer," she said.

"No, same tube, same brand." Cooper turned one in his fingers. Was it the heat? He thought about testing it, but they had only fifteen minutes before Eloi's mom would drive them, so he wrapped the hottest stick in a kitchen towel to insulate it from his warm hand and stuck the dim one in his pocket close to his skin. A pocket experiment, running all night.

At the dance, the gym was a cave of pounding speakers and swinging lights. Cooper handed the cold stick to Lilah, who cracked it and wore it as a bracelet. By nine o'clock, her ghost-green was still glowing, steady and stubborn. His hot one, the one that had blazed like a beacon at seven, had faded to almost nothing. He held them side by side under the bleachers and grinned. Warm meant brighter, but it burned out faster. Cold meant dimmer, but it lasted. It was like the stick was spending its light all at once or saving it up, and the temperature decided which.

He was so absorbed that he didn't notice the slow song until Lilah tapped his shoulder, and the embarrassment of standing there with two dying sticks while everyone paired off hit him hard. He shoved them in his pockets and danced badly on purpose, which made her laugh instead of leaving.

Afterward, back at Eloi's house with pizza, Cooper pulled out the sticks to show them. Lilah's was still glowing faintly after five hours. Then she jumped up, opened the freezer, and wedged hers between the ice trays. "If cold makes them last longer," she said, "this one might still be glowing at breakfast."

"Nine o'clock, my kitchen, everyone bring sunglasses," Eloi said.

In the morning, frost had feathered the freezer door. Lilah peeled the stick out with a dish towel and held it up to the window. A thin green pulse still burned inside the plastic, and Cooper leaned in until his nose almost touched it.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Japan, slurping noodles such as ramen and soba is considered acceptable at the table rather than rude.
story:
Harper stood on Oakley's porch holding a box of mochi she had picked out herself, because her mother had said never arrive at a family dinner empty-handed. She rang the bell twice before she understood that the second ring had been a mistake, and when the door opened, Oakley's grandmother pressed her palms together and bowed. Harper, clutching the box like a shield, did not know whether to bow back or shake hands or wave. She chose a small bow, and the grandmother smiled and took the mochi with both hands, which made Harper wonder if she had done something right on the first try.

Inside, the table was already set for ramen. Oakley's father came in from the kitchen carrying a steaming bowl in each hand, setting them down one at a time, and everyone said what sounded like "itadakimasu" before touching their chopsticks. Harper copied the word half a beat late, like a singer joining a song in the middle. Then the slurping began.

It started with Oakley's little brother, a polite-looking kid who suddenly inhaled his noodles with a sound like a drain unclogging. Harper froze with her chopsticks halfway to her mouth. In her own house, slurping was practically a crime, the kind of thing her grandfather commented on for the rest of dinner. Yet here Oakley's mother slurped, and her father slurped, and even the grandmother, so small and dignified, produced a noise that would have launched a siege of corrections at Harper's table. Nobody glanced at anybody. Nobody apologized. It was the equivalent of saying please and thank you, done with the whole face buried in the bowl.

Harper decided to test it. She lifted a tangle of noodles, waited a second, and slurped as quietly as she could manage, trying to evade notice while still doing the thing. Oakley looked up. "You don't have to be shy about it," Oakley said, laughing. "In Japan, slurping ramen and soba is acceptable. It's not rude like at your house."

Harper slurped again, louder this time, and the sound she made was enormous, and nobody flinched. Oakley's father nodded at her approvingly, and the grandmother refilled her tea before Harper had even asked.

Later, sitting on the floor of Oakley's room while they waited for the mochi, Harper thought about all the dinners where she had whispered "excuse me" for sounds ten times smaller than this. Maybe the rules she had memorized were only one family's rules, one house's. She unwrapped a piece of green tea mochi and took a bite. "Next time at my place," she said, "we're definitely having ramen."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A claim can be checkable even if nobody has checked it yet; 'most students at our school walk to school' could be tested with a survey.
story:
Aaron slumped at his lab table in the science classroom and watched Mr. Yip write a question on the board: "How do students at our school really get to school?" Behind him, Riaan was already talking. "Most students walk," Riaan said. "Everybody knows that."

"Everybody thinks it," said Clementine, without looking up from her notebook. "That's not the same."

Aaron felt the familiar dread of being asked to sort out an argument, because Riaan and Clementine never stopped until someone sided with one of them. He turned around anyway. "How do you know most students walk?"

"I see tons of kids walking every morning," Riaan said.

"That's an opinion," Clementine said. "You saw some kids. Some isn't most."

Aaron picked up his pencil and rolled it between his fingers. He was thinking about the mock trial they had done in social studies, where the defendant had been declared innocent only after the jury saw actual evidence, not just what witnesses felt sure about. "Here's the thing," he said slowly. "Riaan's claim could be checked. Like, actually counted. Nobody has checked it yet, but it could be. That's different from an opinion."

Mr. Yip, who had been straightening the beakers at the front bench, walked over. "Go on," he said, which made Aaron nervous, because Mr. Yip usually only said that when he wanted more than Aaron had.

"We could do a survey," Aaron said. "Ask every student how they get here. Walk, bus, car, bike. Then count it up." He wrote the word survey on the corner of his notebook and underlined it twice.

Riaan leaned back on his stool. "Fine. But you can't ask the whole school in one day."

"We can ask our grade today," Clementine said. She was already folding a sheet of paper into a tally chart with three columns. "Start at lunch."

At lunch, the three of them stood at the end of the cafeteria line with the chart. Riaan asked the questions, Clementine made the marks, and Aaron kept a running total on his calculator. Some students gave strange answers. One boy said his dad drove him on rainy days but he walked otherwise, and a girl named her route as if it were a hereditary trait, saying her whole family had taken the same path for thirty years. Aaron counted her as a walker, then crossed it out, then counted her again as half.

By the end of lunch they had forty-three responses, and walkers were winning by six. Aaron looked at the tally marks and at the three grades they hadn't even started on. "We need the seventh graders," he said, and headed for the door.

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: A person who has memorized the entire Quran, all 114 chapters, is called a hafiz, and keeping it perfectly remembered takes constant practice.
story:
Amelia sat cross-legged on her grandmother's carpet, the afternoon light making the room smell like warm dust and cardamom from the kitchen. In her lap lay the page she was supposed to memorize, the same surah she would recite at her coming-of-age ceremony in three weeks. Every time she reached the middle verse, the words slipped away like water through her fingers.

"Again," she whispered, and got halfway before the line dissolved.

Last summer, she remembered, her cousin had sat on this exact carpet and recited for what felt like an hour without opening a book. Amelia had been ten then, half listening, half amazed, and she had assumed his memory was simply better than hers, a random gift some people got and others didn't.

Now her grandmother's front door opened and the cousin himself walked in, older, carrying a duffel bag. "Amelia! Still fighting with that surah?"

"You made it look easy," she said.

He laughed and sat down across from her. "You know I didn't learn it from a page like that."

She frowned. "What do you mean?"

He tapped his temple. "Everything. The whole Quran, all 114 chapters, up here. Took years." He said it plainly, not bragging.

"There's a word for that," her grandmother called from the kitchen, and then her cousin said it at the same time: "Hafiz."

Amelia leaned forward. "But you learned it years ago. It stays just like that?"

He shook his head slowly. "I recite every single day. If I skip even a week, pieces start to blur. It's like the bank and a mortgage, the grandmother put it later at dinner; you have to keep paying or you lose the house."

Amelia decided to test this. That evening she recited the surah from memory once, then locked the page in her grandmother's wooden cabinet and promised herself not to peek until morning. At breakfast she stood by the window, the smell of buttered toast thick around her, and tried the middle verse. It was gone, exactly where it always vanished. She tried walking the length of the rug while reciting, saying the verse forward and then backward, and on the fourth pass the missing words rose up whole, surprising her like a fish breaking the surface of a pond.

At the ceremony three weeks later, she stood in front of everyone with her hands shaking and delivered every line without a single mistake. Afterward, her grandmother pressed the old carpet's corner into Amelia's hands, a rolled piece to take home, and said quietly, "It was always meant for the one who kept trying."

Amelia carried the roll to the car, knowing she would have to recite every day now, forever, or watch it all slip away. From the porch her cousin called out, "Same time tomorrow?"

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Muscle soreness after new or hard exercise usually peaks 24 to 72 hours later, not right away; this is called delayed onset muscle soreness.
story:
Raphael's first soccer practice of the season ended with him sprinting laps until his lungs burned, and he jogged home feeling great. He flopped onto the backyard grass, peeled off his cleats, and texted Kayleigh: "Coach is tough but I'm fine. Barely tired." She replied with a suspicious row of question marks, which he ignored.

Two mornings later he woke up and nearly fell down the stairs. His thighs ached so deeply that he had to lower himself onto the couch one leg at a time, gripping the railing. He limped into the backyard, where Charbel was waiting to practice passing. "What happened to you?" Charbel asked. "You were fine Monday." Raphael lowered himself onto the picnic bench like an old man and frowned. He hadn't been hurt at practice. Nothing had twisted or snapped. The soreness had arrived out of nowhere, a whole day later, which made no sense to him.

"Maybe you're sick," Charbel said. Raphael shook his head. No fever, no sniffles, just muscles that screamed when he tried to stand. "A virus needs an organism to spread in," he said, thinking aloud, "but nobody else on the team texted that they were sick, and I'd be running a fever." He dragged himself up and tried a slow lap around the yard. The movement hurt at first, then loosened him a little. He stopped, eyes narrowed. "Wait. I felt nothing Monday. It peaked today. Two days after." Charbel pulled out his phone and typed fast. "My cousin's a trainer. She says it's called delayed onset muscle soreness. New or hard exercise, and it peaks 24 to 72 hours later, not right away." Raphael pointed at him. "That's exactly what happened. Not a virus."

He turned the idea over while he poked a ball back and forth with Charbel, slowly, wincing less each minute. The timing implied something useful: if Monday's practice had planted this soreness, then Wednesday's soreness had been set in motion before he even felt it. Which meant Friday's practice would plant Saturday's misery. So Thursday, he decided, he would warm up gently, stretch, and tell the coach his legs were still recovering from the first session, instead of pretending to be invincible and sprinting himself into next week's pain.

Friday's practice still hurt, but not like Monday's, because Raphael paced himself and drank water between every drill. On Saturday morning he walked downstairs normally, smiled at the banister, and carried his ball out to the backyard, where the morning light turned the dew opaque silver on the grass. Kayleigh was already there, juggling the ball on her knees. "Stairs?" she asked. Raphael trapped the ball under his foot and grinned. "Stairs are nothing. Watch this."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: The word "propaganda" comes from a Catholic Church committee for spreading the faith, the Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622.
story:
William climbed onto the 42 bus with his vocabulary sheet folded in his back pocket, holding the pole as the doors hissed shut. His assignment was to look up the history of five words, and four of them had been boring. The fifth word, propaganda, was supposed to be his last stop before Kalen's house, where they were building a model bridge out of coffee stirrers. The bus smelled like rain and vinyl, and a man near the front was humming along with his headphones even though nobody else could hear the song.

Above the windows, an ad showed a famous basketball player holding a purple sports drink. "Everybody's switching," the ad said in enormous letters. William stared at it. Everybody was a strong claim for a bus. He tried to picture everybody, all the people in the world, holding purple drinks, and decided the probability of that was close to zero. The player was grinning like the drink had personally rescued him from something.

Two rows ahead, Kameron from his science class sat with an older boy William didn't know, and Kameron was nodding along as the boy talked. "That neighborhood is full of criminals," the boy said, loud enough that a woman with a grocery bag glanced over. "Total disaster. Everyone knows it." William noticed how the words did work, heavy words, pushing a feeling onto a place William had never even visited. Kameron nodded again, faster.

At his stop, William found Kalen at the kitchen table with the laptop already open, glue on his fingers. "Look," Kalen said, spinning the screen around before William could even sit. He had found the word history first. "Guess where propaganda comes from. Guess." William guessed a war, a president, a newspaper. Kalen shook his head, grinning. "A church committee. The Congregatio de Propaganda Fide, set up by Pope Gregory XV in 1622, for spreading the faith."

William sat down slowly. "So it started as just spreading an idea, like seeds or something." He thought about the basketball player, and the boy on the bus, and the enormous word everybody. "The drink ad never cites any proof that the drink works. It just says a star likes it and that everyone's doing it. That's the same trick, kind of. A gradual one, where you don't even notice." Kalen dotted glue along a stirrer and pressed it into the bridge. "So tomorrow, when Kameron repeats that criminal stuff, what do you say?"

"I ask him where he heard it," William said. "And whether he's ever actually been there." He picked up a stirrer and held it against the tower, checking the angle. Kalen handed him the glue.

"That side's going to sag," Kalen said.

"Only if we let it," said William, and pressed the stick down until it held.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: To change a speed in meters per second into kilometers per hour, multiply it by 3.6.
story:
Riley crouched beside the long ramp in the gymnasium, marking it with tape every half meter, because her project was due at the science fair in exactly two hours and her first ramp had turned out to be crooked. The gym smelled like floor wax and popcorn from the concession table. Leyla held the meter stick steady while Catalina, who had appointed herself timekeeper, clicked the stopwatch experimentally.

"Do it again," Riley said. "You stopped the clock before I let go of the ball."

"That's called anticipation," said Catalina. "Athletes have it."

They ran the ball down the ramp six times. Riley recorded each trial in her notebook, distance in meters along the left column and time in seconds along the right, then plotted the points on graph paper. When she connected them, the line was nearly straight, climbing steadily from the origin, and she felt a small quiet satisfaction. A straight line through the origin meant the ball's speed had stayed constant, which meant she could actually calculate it. She took her best trial, two meters in 1.6 seconds, and divided. One point two five.

"Point two five what?" Leyla asked, peering over her shoulder.

"Meters per second. That's my speed." Riley frowned at the number anyway. Something about it bothered her, and she tried to formulate exactly what. The units themselves were the problem, she decided. Meters per second meant nothing to most people walking past a poster.

"You know what you should do?" said Catalina, who had wandered over from the popcorn table with a full bag. "Figure out if your ball beats a person walking. Like a race. People get that."

Riley considered the context. A walking person went about five kilometers per hour, her dad had once said on one of their hikes, and she happened to know her ball's speed in meters per second, and the two had to be comparable somehow. There was a conversion, she was almost sure. She flipped through her math notebook from the beginning of the semester, past the fertile pages of half-finished homework where good ideas had sprouted and then been abandoned, until she found it in her own handwriting, circled twice: to change a speed in meters per second into kilometers per hour, multiply by 3.6.

She did it twice to be sure. One point two five times 3.6 came out to 4.5 kilometers per hour. She sat back on her heels. The walking person won. Her ball, which had looked so swift rolling down the ramp, would lose a race to someone strolling to the bus stop.

"Well?" Catalina crunched popcorn.

"Four point five kilometers per hour," Riley said. "A walker does five."

Leyla laughed so hard she had to put down the meter stick. "Your ball loses to my grandmother."

Mr. Haile, checking tables down the row, paused at theirs. "You converted that yourself?" he asked, tapping the notebook page. Riley nodded. He looked at her graph, then at the ramp, and asked whether the ball would go faster on a steeper one, and whether her graph would still be a straight line.

Riley looked at the stack of books under the high end of the ramp, then at the clock. Ninety minutes until judging. Catalina was already pulling out the bottom book.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: The 2003 book "Moneyball" by Michael Lewis described how the 2002 Oakland Athletics used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players.
story:
Tyler kept his notebook open on his knee as the school bus rattled past the hardware store. In it he had copied the box score from last night's basketball game, because Raelynn insisted Devonne was the best player on the team and Tyler thought she was wrong. Devonne averaged fourteen points a game. Marcus averaged eleven. But Tyler had watched every game this season, and something about those numbers felt like a photograph of a room where all the furniture had been moved.

"You're counting again," Raelynn said, dropping into the seat across the aisle. Aryanna leaned over her shoulder to look. "Fourteen beats eleven. That's just math."

"Fourteen is one number for eight games," Tyler said. "It squashes everything together." He tapped his pencil down the column of Devonne's points: 28, 3, 25, 6, 30, 2, 24, 14. Half the games were huge and half were nearly nothing. Marcus's column was boring and steady, 10, 12, 11, 9, 13, 10, 12, 13. Tyler circled the middle numbers. "The median tells a different story. Devonne's is about fourteen, same as his average. Marcus's is 11, same as his. That's not it either." He chewed the pencil eraser. So what was he actually trying to see?

He thought of his uncle at the sports bar two weeks ago, the night the whole family had crowded around the screen. "Read this," his uncle had said, sliding a paperback across the table. "Michael Lewis wrote it. Moneyball, 2003." Tyler had flipped it over while his uncle kept going, quieter now, almost to himself: "The Oakland Athletics, back in 2002, used statistics like on-base percentage to find undervalued players." A low-budget team competing with rich teams by looking at numbers nobody else trusted. Tyler had been hesitant to believe it at the time, one number outperforming millions of dollars, but the idea had stuck to him ever since, orbiting his brain like a satellite he couldn't shake.

"What's on-base percentage?" Aryanna asked now, reading his mind, or maybe his face.

"How many times a player gets on base instead of making an out," Tyler said. "It counts walks. Points don't." He looked back at his notebook, and the page seemed to rearrange itself. He had a column for shots but not one for passes. Devonne shot every time he touched the ball. When the score was close and the shot missed, the ball seemed to orbit the rim and bounce out, and Devonne's teammate would be standing alone under the basket, unguarded, every single time. Tyler started a new column with a ruler, straight and careful, and headed it with Marcus's name.

"Whatever you're doing," Raelynn said, "you're doing it at the tournament too."

"Get me the stat sheet," Tyler said, already flipping to a clean page as the bus hissed to a stop.

activity: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
knowledge_domain: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
fact: German can form the future with "werden" plus an infinitive at the end of the sentence, as in "Ich werde Deutsch lernen," meaning "I will learn German."
story:
Amelia sat at the kitchen table with her German book open to a blank page. The assignment was simple enough: a paragraph about her plans for next year, all in the future tense. Mr. Ho had written one example on the board before the bell, and she had copied it down without really looking at it. Now she looked. "Ich werde Deutsch lernen." Two words she recognized, werden and lernen, and the rest she would have to build herself.

She tried her first sentence. "Ich werde gehe nach Berlin." Something about it felt wrong, the way a crooked picture frame feels wrong before you see the tilt. She read it aloud, and her voice slowed at gehe. It sounded like she had said "I will go go." She flipped back through her notes and found the example again. In Mr. Ho's sentence, the verb lernen sat at the very end, after Deutsch. In her sentence, gehe sat in the middle, right after werde, like it belonged there because English worked that way.

Her phone buzzed. Musa had sent a photo of his own paragraph, and his sentences had the same shape as hers, verbs crowding the middle. She typed back, "Look at the example he wrote. The main verb goes last." Then, to verify it, she checked two more sentences in the textbook chapter. Ich werde ein Buch lesen. Ich werde meine Oma besuchen. The pattern held every time: werden, then everything else, then the infinitive at the end.

Outside the window, the gray stone wall of the house was spotted with lichen, pale green circles that had spread since the rainy month. Her dad had said last spring he would scrub it off and then never had, and the wall had quietly gone on growing its own map. Amelia thought about how often she did the same thing, saying she would do something and then letting it slide. Last term she had been almost negligent about German homework, leaving it until the bus ride, and now here she was, the night before, doing exactly that again. She smoothed the page and kept writing anyway. "Nächstes Jahr werde ich nach Berlin fahren." She read it aloud. "Next year I will to Berlin travel." It sounded strange in English, but in German it had a rhythm, like the verb was a stone dropped at the end of a line.

She finished the paragraph, all six sentences, each one holding its shape. Then she read Musa's reply: "He posted a new example. Check the class page." She opened it. Mr. Ho had added a note under his own example sentence. It said, "Remember, ich werde Deutsch lernen means I will learn German." Amelia stared at her page, at her careful verb-final sentences, and wondered whether she had actually understood the rule or only copied a shape.

The kitchen light hummed. She picked up her pen again and hovered over the last line, then wrote, "Ich werde mehr studieren."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Fire-safety guidance says to put out a campfire by drowning it with water, stirring the ashes, and drowning it again until everything is cool to the touch.
story:
The train had been moving for twenty minutes before Landon stopped staring out the window and started doing math in his head. They had left the campsite at nine, and Dad was staying behind to pack the van and lock up the trailer. He planned to be on the road by eleven. That gave him two hours, which sounded like plenty, except Landon kept picturing the fire pit. They had put it out in a hurry that morning, before the rain started. He had dumped one bucket of water on it, everyone had piled into the car, and nobody had stirred anything.

"You're doing your worried face," said Valentina, who was sitting across from him with her feet on her backpack. She and her mom were taking the same train east, which was the only fun part of the whole trip. "What's wrong?"

"The fire," Landon said. "I only drowned it once. There was still smoke coming off the edge when we walked away."
