He had learned the right way back in June, from a booklet at the ranger station: to put out a campfire you drown it with water, stir the ashes, and drown it again, and you keep doing that until everything is cool to the touch. One bucket and no stirring was not that. It wasn't a trivial mistake either, the kind you shrug off. Buried under grey ash there could still be an ember, and he couldn't see it from a moving train, which was the whole problem. Hidden causes were like that, his science teacher would have said, though Mr. Pelletier would also have made them diagram it.

"Call your dad," Valentina said.

Landon retrieved his phone from the side pocket of his pack and found one bar of service flickering between hills. He dialed anyway. It rang four times, long enough for him to imagine the van already pulling onto the highway, the fire pit abandoned with its secret heat.

"Dad, wait. Before you leave. The fire pit."

"I'm looking at it right now," Dad said.

"You have to drown it, stir the ashes, and drown it again. Keep going until everything's cool to the touch. Not just warm. Cool."

"I know," Dad said. There was a scraping sound, metal against stone. "I did the first round an hour ago, and I've been back twice since. The sticks were hissing when I stirred them, so I poured a whole second bucket. I was about to do a third because the big log at the back still feels warm to my hand." A pause, then the sound of water splashing, and the line crackled. "There. Everything's cool now. Even the ring."

Landon let out a breath. "Okay. Good."

"Goodbye, Landon. Train's fine?" Dad asked, and Landon said it was, and they hung up.

Valentina raised her eyebrows. "So your dad was already on it."

"Yeah." Landon slumped back against the seat. Two hours of worrying over an ember he couldn't see, and Dad had been standing in the rain, patiently drowning a dead fire. Valentina started laughing, and after a second he did too.

"Next time," she said, "call before the train leaves."

activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
knowledge_domain: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
fact: Scientists estimate the Colorado River began carving the Grand Canyon about 5 to 6 million years ago.
story:
Cameron had a tray of dirt on the kitchen table, a jug of water, and one very suspicious cat. He was supposed to be writing a paragraph about the Grand Canyon for Monday, and the paragraph was supposed to include how long the river took. He'd written "a while" and then crossed it out.

The trouble had started that afternoon in Ms. He's class, when she'd held up a postcard of the canyon and asked them to explain how a river could carve a hole that deep. Cameron had said, confidently, "It's basically a big flood." Alicia had looked at him the way you look at a pizza that's fallen cheese-side down. Kruz had just said, "Sure, a flood that lasted forever," which was somehow worse, because it made Cameron's answer sound wrong twice at once. Ms. He hadn't corrected anyone. She'd only said, "Find out," and Cameron suspected she enjoyed that.

Now, at home, he poured a slow stream of water across the tray of dirt. At first nothing happened. He tilted the tray, and the water found one groove and sank into it, widening it, dragging tiny crumbs of dirt downhill in a muddy smear. It wasn't dramatic. That was the thing. It was slow, patient, almost boring, and yet the groove got deeper every minute. He nudged the tray steeper, remembering a video he'd watched where a scientist said the Colorado River began carving the Grand Canyon about 5 to 6 million years ago. Five to six million years. His groove had taken four minutes. He tried the math on the back of his hand and decided not to write the number down, in case it was ridiculous, which it was.

Last summer, at his grandfather's house, there had been a gully behind the fence that the grown-ups all complained about after every storm. Cameron had thought the storm made it, because the storm was volatile, all thunder and drama, while ordinary days seemed to conceal their work completely. But now he looked at his tray and understood he'd had it backward. The loud thing moved the dirt, sure, but the quiet water was the one that never stopped. The gully was the storm's plan, carried out by the drizzle.

He built a flat-topped ridge of dirt, a little plateau, and cut a channel down its middle, then ran the water again. Sediment piled up at the bottom where the slope eased, a tiny muddy delta, deposition happening right there between the salt shaker and the cat.

"Enjoying the show?" he asked the cat. The cat blinked. Cameron wrote one sentence at the top of his page: "Rivers don't tear things open; they persuade them, grain by grain." Then he poured again, and the plateau's edge, ever so slightly, crumbled.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Pigs have very few working sweat glands, so they wallow in mud or water to cool off on hot days.
story:
The fire station sat at the edge of town, and beyond its back fence Maelie could see a small farm where three pink pigs stood panting in a shaded corner of their pen. The class had come to see the trucks, and Mr. Halvorsen, who once worked here and still had a key, was letting them climb aboard Engine 4. "One at a time," he said. "There's a hierarchy to these things. Driver, officer, then everybody else." Dane groaned because he wanted the driver's seat, and Skyla, who was third in line, kept checking her phone battery like the photo she planned to take might expire.

Maelie took her turn in the officer's seat, but her eyes kept drifting out the window. It was the hottest day of the summer so far, and the pigs were plastered in mud so thick and opaque that she couldn't tell where the mud ended and the pig began. Were they just messy animals? she wondered. But why would they stand in muck on purpose on a day like this, when the whole rest of the pen was clean and shaded?

While the others lined up at the pole, Maelie slipped to the back fence with her water bottle from lunch. If the pigs were dirty because they liked dirt, they'd ignore water. She poured a splash into the dry dirt near the fence, making a small puddle, and waited. The biggest pig trotted over, flopped down, and rolled until its whole side glistened. It wasn't the dirt, Maelie thought. It was wet. The mud was just a way to stay wet longer.

She found Mr. Halvorsen by the hose rack. "The pigs next door," she said. "Are they rolling in mud to cool off?" He nodded. "Pigs have very few working sweat glands," he said, "so they wallow in mud or water on hot days." Maelie wanted to verify that, so she asked if she could borrow the small hose for a minute. He checked with the duty firefighter, who shrugged and said the connection by the back gate was fine.

She sprayed a thin arc over the fence while Dane, having finally claimed the driver's seat, leaned out the truck window to watch. The three pigs jogged to the fence, and when the water pooled in the low spot of their pen, they lay down in it one by one, grunting, ribs heaving, cooler already. Skyla squeezed through the gate with her phone raised. "Move the hose a little left," she said. "I want the rainbow in the picture."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: iPhones and Android phones let you choose, app by app, whether an app may use your location always, only while you are using it, or never.
story:
Alexandre had one hour before the mall's gaming tournament started, and he meant to spend it finding the leak. Two weeks ago he had posted a photo of his sneakers here, at Riverside Mall, and by that evening three strangers had commented asking if he was "the kid who hangs out by the fountain every Saturday." He had never written that. He had never posted a schedule. Yet somehow the pattern was out there, stored somewhere, visible to people he did not know.

Cassidy met him near the fountain, phone in hand. "So what's the plan? You check the photo itself?"

"The photo's just a picture," Alexandre said. "But when I posted it, the app knew where I was. That's my inference. Something on my phone is telling them." He scrolled through his settings while shoppers streamed past the storefronts, and found the screen he'd only half-remembered. Each app had its own choice, app by app: whether it may use his location always, only while he was using it, or never.

"Wait, you can pick that?" Cassidy leaned over. "Per app?"

"Always, only while using, or never," Alexandre read. "Every app, one by one." He tapped into the map app he used for bus times. Only while using. Fine. His camera. Never. Then a free puzzle game, one Cassidy had begged him to try last month, the one with the cheerful cartoon monsters. The little arrow beside it said Always.

"Every Saturday," Cassidy said slowly. "You play it while we wait for the tournament line."

"And it's been telling the game's company where I am, even when I'm not playing." Alexandre felt the floor tilt a little, the way it does when something ordinary turns out to have been watching you. He changed it to Never, and the arrow went gray.

At the tournament table, Penelope waved them over, and a boy Alexandre didn't recognize was already there, wearing a counterfeit jersey with a crooked logo stitched over the number. "You're the fountain guy," the boy said. "I saw your picture. Cool shoes. You here every week, right?"

Alexandre looked at him, deciding in one breath. "Not anymore," he said. "Same mall, but you won't know when." It wasn't a lie exactly, though it cost him something to say it, because the fountain line had been the good part of Saturdays, the part strangers had shared with him without his knowing.

After the matches, he checked the game's app one more time, half expecting the setting to have crept back to Always, the way some things quietly do. Never, it still said. He slid the phone into his pocket and turned toward the fountain, where Cassidy was saving his place in line, and where nobody, as far as he could tell, was keeping count anymore.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: In one-point perspective, objects of the same real size, like lampposts along a street, are drawn smaller and closer together the farther away they are.
story:
Penelope sat on the porch of her grandfather's house with a sketchpad on her knees, trying to draw the street that curved past the front gate. Her first attempt lay beside her, and every time she looked at it, her stomach sank a little. The street didn't look like a street at all. It looked like a flat wall with lines painted on it. She had drawn the lampposts marching down the middle, every single one the same height, evenly spaced like fence pickets, and the whole picture had refused to lie down flat on the page.

She thought about her grandfather, who had spent his whole life in agriculture and who could look at a field of wheat and tell you, without walking out to it, whether the far rows were healthy. When she'd asked him how, he said the far rows looked different, lighter and closer together, and your eye learned to mediate between what you saw and what you knew was there. She had laughed at him then. Now she wondered whether drawing a street worked the same way, like there was a rule hiding somewhere that her eyes hadn't learned yet.

Pierre-Olivier pedaled up the drive and dropped his bike in the gravel. "That's not a street," he said, looking over her shoulder at the flat wall. "It's a picture of a street that got squashed."

"I know it's wrong," Penelope said. "I just can't see where it went wrong." She flipped to a fresh page and drew two lines that started wide at the bottom of the page and slanted toward each other until they nearly touched near the top. Then she made a small dot where they almost met. She had heard the word once, in a hallway, from a kid who took art on Tuesdays. "Vanishing point," she said, mostly to herself.

She set her pencil at the top of the nearest lamppost and drew a faint guide line from it to the dot. Then she tried the same thing from a lamppost farther down the street, and the guide line cut lower across the page. She placed a dot where it landed and drew a post there, smaller. She did it again, farther along, and again, and the posts came out smaller and closer together the deeper into the page they went, even though she knew they were all the same real height, because she could see them standing equal outside the gate.

When she finished, she held the pad out at arm's length. The street ran away from her, deep and real, the posts shrinking into the distance exactly the way the real ones did past the gate. Pierre-Olivier leaned in, then looked up at the actual street, then back at the page. "It goes back," he said. "Mine never did that." He ran inside to get his own paper, and Penelope heard him calling for a pencil before the screen door had even banged shut.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage, adjourning, for when a group finishes its work and breaks up.
story:
At the end-of-season party in Lillian's backyard, nobody was eating the cake. The Rockets had gone undefeated in soccer, Coach had brought a trophy the size of a toaster, and still everyone stood around the picnic table like they were waiting for something bad to happen. Lillian watched Ishaan kick a pinecone against the fence, over and over, and watched Sophie turn her water bottle slowly in her hands without drinking. It didn't make sense. They had won. So why did the whole team feel like a plate someone had tapped, that brittle hum right before it cracks?

"It's not the losing teams that cry at awards day," Lillian said to Sophie. "I checked. The winning ones cry too."

Sophie shrugged. "Maybe everybody's just tired."

Lillian didn't think so. That night she dug through her older sister's old books from a business class, the ones with chapters about how people work in groups, and there it was. A researcher named Tuckman had described the stages a group goes through, forming, storming, norming, performing, and for years that was where it ended. Then in 1977 Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added a fifth stage. It was called adjourning, for when a group finishes its work and breaks up. Lillian read the page twice, then closed the book carefully, like it might fall apart in her hands.

The next morning she called Ishaan. "Meet me in the backyard at ten. Bring Sophie."

When they came, she had a plan. If the sad feeling was really the fifth stage, then it should show up wherever a group broke up, not just their team. "I'm going to document it," she said, holding up a notebook. "Every team, every club, everything that ends. We test it." They made a list. Ishaan's cousin had worked at a corporation all summer in an office and had moped for a week when her project team finished and everyone went back to different desks. Sophie's book club had ended in June, and the members still texted each other photos of books they thought the others would like. Even Lillian's dad's garage band, which had practiced for years, had gone quiet for a month after their last gig.

"That's four out of four," Ishaan said, counting the notebook pages.

"Five," Lillian said. "Counting us."

So on Saturday she brought the notebook to the field where the Rockets were having their last pickup game before summer. She stood in front of the team, feeling her ears go hot, and said, "It's called adjourning. It's the last stage. In 1977 this guy Tuckman and Mary Ann Jensen added it, for when a group finishes its work and breaks up. That's what's happening to us. That's why the cake party felt so weird."

Nobody laughed, which she had feared. A girl named Ishaan passed the ball to Sophie, who trapped it and looked at Lillian for a long second.

"Then we're in it right now," Sophie said. "Last game. Everybody in?"

They played until the grass stains went past their knees. Afterward, sweating and laughing, they crowded around the notebook, and one by one every player signed the page under the word Lillian had written at the top: Adjourning.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Line dances, in which a group repeats the same set of steps facing the same direction, let people dance together without needing a partner.
story:
The dance started in ninety minutes, and Nicolas was lying on Samira's living room floor with a pillow over his face. "Everyone already has a partner," he said through the pillow. "Aleena's going with that kid from her math class. You have a partner. I have nothing."

Samira snatched the pillow away. "Get up. You've been doom-spiraling for twenty minutes and we still have to get ready." Her little cousin was in the corner of the room, doing something with her feet that looked like a mix of marching and hopscotch. She stomped, clapped, turned, stomped again, all facing the big window.

Nicolas watched her. "What is she doing?"

"A line dance. My aunt taught her. It's from her side of the family, part of her heritage, and she will do it anywhere, including the grocery store." Samira raised her voice. "Show him the whole thing."

The cousin lined up three stuffed animals beside her, all facing the same direction as her, then did the steps again. Stomp, clap, turn, stomp. The animals just sat there, but somehow it looked like a group.

"Wait," Nicolas said slowly, sitting up. "She's not dancing with anybody. She's just doing the same steps as everyone else, facing the same way. If a whole crowd did that, nobody would need a partner at all." He counted on his fingers. "There are what, four moves? Four moves and you're dancing with thirty people."

"Line dances," Samira said, "let a whole group do the same steps together facing the same direction. Nobody needs a partner. That is literally the entire point." She pulled him to his feet. "So you have a job now. Learn four steps before the car leaves."

They pushed the coffee table aside to accommodate a practice area, which mostly meant the cousin shouting "AGAIN" every time Nicolas messed up the turn. The footwork felt intricate at first, like his shoes were tied together, but by the tenth try his feet found the pattern. Stomp, clap, turn, stomp. He did it facing the couch, facing the kitchen, facing the front door, just to prove it worked in every direction, and Samira cracked up when he whispered "stomp, clap" at her mother's houseplant.

In the car, Nicolas practiced with his hands on his knees. At the gym doors he could already hear the bass, and his stomach did one slow flip. Then the music changed, and a voice on the speakers called out, "Okay, everybody, line up!"

The whole floor turned the same direction at once, strangers and couples and kids from every grade, and Nicolas slid into the back row just as the stomping started.

"Stomp, clap," he said out loud, and grinned at Samira across the gym.

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev published an early version of the periodic table in 1869.
story:
Sophie had taped her periodic table poster to the gym wall six times before it finally stayed put, and by the time the science fair doors opened, she could hear the poster paper flapping like it wanted to escape. Her project was called "Counting the Invisible," and the whole idea had come to her three weeks ago when she'd realized that no one, not once, had ever actually seen a proton. Yet there they were on every element card, counted as confidently as candies in a jar.

"Table four, table four," said Emerson, who was stationed at the next table with a homemade volcano. "The judges are heading this way, and one of them has a clipboard, which we all know means business."

Sophie straightened her element cards. She had made one for every element in the first three rows, and on the back of each she had written a single number. Carbon had a 6. Neon had a 10. Sodium had an 11. The trick, she had discovered, was hiding in plain sight on the front of each card: the tiny number in the corner of each box on the periodic table was the atomic number, and the atomic number was exactly how many protons the element had. She had tested it on a dozen elements with the library's reference book, and every single time the numbers matched.

The clipboard judge stopped at her table. "So, young lady, what's invisible here?"

"Protons," Sophie said. "You can't see them, but you can count them. Pick any card."

The judge picked oxygen. Sophie flipped it over: 8. "Eight protons. The atomic number tells you, every time, no guessing. That's the pattern nobody had to discover by looking, because you can't look."

Behind the judge, a boy from another school, Nicolas, was leaning over the museum timeline Ms. Clarke's class had brought as a display. "Hey," he called out, pointing at a faded reproduction of an old handwritten chart. "This thing only has about sixty elements on it. Were people just lazy back then?"

Sophie came around the table to look. The timeline card under the chart read: Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev published an early version of the periodic table in 1869.

"That's Mendeleev," Sophie said. "The early version. They hadn't found them all yet."

"Found them, or made them?" Nicolas asked.

"Found. Some of them are hiding in rocks, in tiny amounts, and chemists had to extract them, like digging a marble out of a bucket of sand." She tapped the chart's empty gaps. "And look, he left blanks. He thought there should be something there."

The clipboard judge was writing fast now. "You tested your proton rule against reference data?"

"Twelve elements," Sophie said. "I want to do all of them. I figured out how, too. If I line up my cards by atomic number and find the median, I can split them into two piles and check each pile the same way."

Ms. Clarke appeared behind the judge, arms crossed, smiling in that way she had when she was deciding something. "Sophie, the regional fair is in March. Registration closes Friday."

The poster chose that moment to peel loose and swing down over the timeline. Nicolas laughed, Sophie grabbed for it, and the judge said, "Hold that thought, I'm coming back with the head judge."

Sophie smoothed the poster flat and looked at all those numbered boxes, sixty in Mendeleev's chart, more in hers, the whole invisible world lined up and counted. "Friday," she said to Emerson. "I'm registering tonight."

activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
knowledge_domain: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
fact: Faster water can carry bigger particles; when a river slows down, it drops its load, with the largest pieces settling first.
story:
Charlie had exactly twenty minutes to figure out the Grand Canyon before Mr. López collected everyone at the museum exit, and she was not going to waste one of them.

"Look at this," she said, dragging Aksel and Winter toward the stream table in the erosion hall. Workers had installed it that morning, a long slanted tray with a hose at the top and a ramp of sand, gravel, and little pebbles waiting to be carved. Aksel grabbed the hose handle before she could.

"Watch," he said, and opened the valve wide. Water rushed down the tray, and within seconds a channel began to cut into the sand, branching like lightning. Charlie leaned over it, nose almost touching the glass. "It's working! The canyon's forming!" The water quickened at the steep middle section, and she noticed something odd. Pebbles that had been sitting near the top were hopping, tumbling, riding the current. But the fine sand barely moved at all from up there. It just slid slowly, in little clouds.

"Wait," Charlie said. "The big rocks are moving and the sand isn't? That's backwards." She snatched the valve from Aksel and slowed the flow to a trickle. The pebbles stopped instantly, dropping where they were, halfway down the tray. But the muddy water kept drifting on, thin and brown, all the way to the bottom of the slope, where it pooled and went still. Only then did the haze settle out, coating the lowest inch of the tray in silky smooth mud.

Winter crouched at the end of the table, eyes wide. "So the pebbles got dropped first and the mud got carried the whole way. That's why they're in different places." Charlie felt her heart thumping like she'd won something. Faster water could haul the heavy stuff, and the moment it slowed, the water let it go, biggest pieces first, finest stuff last. She flipped the valve wide again, then slow, watching the deposits rearrange themselves, pebbles high, mud low, over and over, like the table was telling her a secret in code.

"That's the whole canyon," she said. "Millions of years of this. The river carries, then it slows, then it drops." Mr. López appeared behind them with his clipboard, indifferent to their discovery, already counting heads. But Charlie wasn't moving until the last grain of mud settled. "Ten more seconds," she begged, and Aksel turned the hose on full.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Johann Nepomuk Maelzel patented the mechanical metronome, a ticking device that sets a steady tempo, in 1815.
story:
Joshua's hands were damp on the keys when Ms. Romano set the small wooden box on top of the piano. "Try it once more," she said, "with the machine." The night before, he had found a note folded into his sheet music, in Leyla's round handwriting: "Cory says you rush the fast part every rehearsal. I don't hear it, but he's not wrong about things like this. Please check. Also I saved you a seat at the concert. L." He had read the letter three times, half grateful and half stung, and practiced until ten o'clock without solving anything.

The box had a pendulum inside and a slider you could move up and down. When he set it going, it ticked like a patient insect. Ms. Romano said only, "Maelzel patented this in 1815. It's called a metronome." Then she sat back and let him work.

He started the piece at the slow marking, sixty ticks a minute, and by the eighth measure the ticking and his hands had drifted apart, his fingers running ahead like water finding a downhill path. There it was. He couldn't feel the rushing at all while he played, but the machine could see it for him, or hear it. It was like the time in sixth grade when his bike wobbled and he blamed the road, until his dad pointed at the loose front wheel. The wobble wasn't the road. The rushing wasn't the piece. It was him.

He tried a small experiment. Instead of playing the whole song, he took just the loud, quick passage and set the metronome slower than it should ever go, glacially slow, so every note had room. Then, measure by measure, he raised the tempo by small steps, calibrating the slider until the ticking matched the marking on the page. The speed wasn't a variable he could leave to his mood anymore; it was fixed outside him, steady while his excitement rose and fell. When he finally played the passage through, loud where the dynamics said loud, soft where they said soft, it came out coherent for the first time, all one piece of music instead of pieces glued together.

Ms. Romano smiled at the last chord. "That," she said, "is what I wanted you to find yourself."

At Thursday rehearsal, Cory kept time by tapping his sneaker against the floor, and when the fast part arrived, Joshua stayed with him, note for note, all the way to the end. Leyla caught his eye across the music stand and raised her eyebrows. He tapped his pocket, where he'd written 1815 on a scrap of paper. "New machine," he mouthed, and turned the page.

activity: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
knowledge_domain: to write a paragraph in a new language about plans for next year using the future tense
fact: The French verb "être" (to be) has an irregular future stem, "ser-," so "I will be" is "je serai."
story:
Mr. Lin set the timer for twenty minutes and said the paragraph had to be about plans for next year, all in the future tense. William stared at his lined paper. He had already written his first sentence: "Next year I will be in grade eight." The problem was the French half of the page, which was blank.

"You can't still be on sentence one," Lucca whispered from the next desk. "I've got four lines."

"Because you're writing about pizza," William whispered back. "You only need 'I will eat.'"

Lucca shrugged, as if that were a reasonable strategy. William looked at his verb chart, the one with the endings for the future tense. He knew how to build it. You took the infinitive, added the ending. Parler plus ai made parlerai, I will speak. Finir plus ai made finirai. So "to be," which was être, should give him êtreai. He wrote it down and stopped.

It looked wrong. It sat on the page like the fungus growing on the bread in the science corner, something that shouldn't be there and definitely wasn't French. He crossed it out and wrote it again. Still wrong.

Madalyn leaned over the gap between their desks. "You're making that face."

"There's no such word as êtreai," William said.

"So don't use it."

"I have to. My whole paragraph is about being in grade eight. Being is the first sentence."

He thought about his verb list from September. Avoir, to have, future stem aur. Aller, to go, future stem ir. Those hadn't come from the infinitives either. He'd memorized them without noticing, the way he'd memorized the route to school. So maybe être did the same thing, shed its whole body and grew a new stem. He tried sounds in his head. Ser? He wrote "je serai" in careful, meticulous letters, then checked it against nothing, because there was nothing to check it against. Only the timer, which showed nine minutes left.

At the bell, Mr. Lin walked the rows. When he reached William's desk he paused, tapped the page once, and said, "Je serai. Good."

"You knew that was a guess," William said.

"Doesn't matter. You tested it." Mr. Lin moved on to Lucca's paper. "Lucca. You cannot eat pizza every day next year. Variety."

William slid his paragraph into his binder and looked at Madalyn. "Next year," he said, "I will be the one who finishes first."

"In French?" she said. "Say it in French."

"Je serai," said William, and zipped the binder shut.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: The Rubin vase, introduced by Danish psychologist Edgar Rubin in 1915, can be seen as either a vase or two faces, but not both at the same moment.
story:
Xavier leaned closer to the poster outside Mr. Harper's classroom, tracing the white shape in the middle with one finger. "It's a vase," he said. "Obviously a vase."

Karson crossed his arms. "It's two faces. Two profiles, like they're about to kiss. There's a nose and a chin on each side."

"They can't both be right," Xavier said, though even as he said it, he could feel something shift. The vase seemed to fold inward, and suddenly the curves he'd been following turned into a forehead and a tip of a nose. He blinked hard and the vase came back, but only after he stopped trying to see the faces. "Wait. I see the faces now. But when I see them, the vase is gone."

Stanley wandered over from the water fountain, still wiping his mouth on his sleeve. "Mr. Harper put that up yesterday. It's called a Rubin vase." He tapped the small caption at the bottom of the poster. "Some Danish psychologist named Edgar Rubin came up with it, back in 1915. It can be seen as either a vase or two faces, but not both at the same time."

Xavier read the caption twice. That was the strange part, the part that made his brain itch. He covered the black part with one hand and the white part popped out as a vase. He covered the white edges with his fingers spread wide, and the faces appeared like they'd been hiding there the whole time. He tried to force both at once, staring until his eyes watered. Nothing. It flicked from one to the other like a light switch with no middle position.

"So who's right?" Karson asked.

"Maybe both of us," Xavier said slowly. "We're looking at the exact same poster and seeing totally different pictures." He thought about the argument he'd had with his dad last week, both of them describing the same awful, turbulent car ride home in completely different ways, each one certain the other was wrong. Maybe that worked the same way. Maybe neither of them was lying. "Hold on. I want to try something."

He grabbed a marker from the bin by the door and wrote beneath the caption: WHAT DO YOU SEE? VASE OR FACES? Then, careful to isolate his handwriting so it wouldn't touch the poster itself, he added a tally chart with two columns and left the marker resting on the ledge.

By lunch, the chart was full. Nine tallies for vase, eleven for faces, and a sticky note in messy printing that said, I CAN SWITCH! IT JUST TAKES A SECOND. Karson stood beside him, counting the marks. "Eleven people saw faces first. That means you owe me a chip."

"One condition," Xavier said, snapping the cap back on the marker. "Tomorrow we ask them if they can see the other one too."

Karson handed him the bag anyway.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Snapchat's Snap Map, launched in 2017, can show a user's real-time location to their friends on a map.
story:
Cooper sat in the corner of the gaming store with his tablet balanced on his knee, logged into the lobby where his squad always met at four o'clock. His controller had died during first period, and the only replacement cable in town was on the rack three feet away, still sealed in its translucent plastic. He had exactly nine dollars, and the cable cost eleven, which was the problem driving everything else.

"There he is," Samara's voice came through his earbuds, crackling a little. "Ready for the tournament match?"

"Sort of," Cooper said. "I'm at the mall, actually. I can't play unless I get this cable, and I'm two dollars short." He said it fast, hoping the embarrassment would slide past everyone.

"You're at the mall?" Samara said. "In the game store, right? The one next to the pretzel place, standing by the accessories rack?"

Cooper looked up so fast he nearly dropped the tablet. He had not told anyone where he was. The store window faced the food court, and through it he could see Maddison at a table with her phone, which meant she might have guessed. But Samara was at home, miles away, and she had known his exact position. There had to be a hidden cause, something he could not see directly, and he decided to test it. He walked two aisles over, to the sports games section.

"You moved," Samara said. "Now you're by the sports games."

"How do you keep doing that?" Cooper asked.

Maddison's voice joined the lobby. "It's Snap Map. It's been on Snapchat since 2017, and it shows your real-time location to your friends on a map. Samara's watching your little icon walk around the store."

Cooper pulled out his phone and found the map. His own dot glowed in the middle of a building labeled with the mall's name, and around it he could see Samara's dot at her house and Maddison's dot at the food court, close enough that he could picture her table exactly. He had never thought of it before. A stranger could not see him, but every friend could, any time, whether he wanted them to or not.

He opened his chat and typed a message to Maddison: "Can I borrow two dollars for the cable? I'll pay you back Monday. Also, turning off my map now. It feels weird being a dot."

He pressed send, found the setting, and switched his location to ghost mode. His dot vanished from the map, though Samara would probably tease him about it later.

A reply popped up. "Deal. Meet me at the pretzel place. I'll insulate you from Samara's jokes. She's already typing."

Cooper walked toward the food court, cable money in reach, one invisible thing on his phone finally under his control.

activity: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
knowledge_domain: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
fact: Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles, known as the war guilt clause, made Germany accept responsibility for the loss and damage caused by the war.
story:
The museum's Second World War gallery smelled like floor wax and old paper, and Madison had exactly forty minutes before Mr. Nakamura's class reassembled at the front doors. She stood in front of a display case with a copy of the Treaty of Versailles inside, her notebook open to a blank page.

"I don't get it," said Brennan, peering over her shoulder. "We have to explain how one treaty helped start a whole other war. That's like saying a scraped knee caused a broken leg."

"Mr. Nakamura said to find the factor nobody notices," Madison said. She read the panel beside the case twice. Then she saw it, a short paragraph about Article 231, and she copied the number down and underlined it. "Listen. Article 231 made Germany accept responsibility for the loss and damage caused by the war."

"So what? Somebody always signs the papers."

Madison tapped the glass. "Everybody blamed Germany. Only Germany. They even called it the war guilt clause." She said the words slowly, because something was clicking into place, the way a math problem suddenly worked when you stopped rushing. "Imagine our group project fails, and the teacher blames only you. Not me, not Amari, just you."

Brennan frowned. "I'd be furious. Especially if we all messed it up."

"And would you want to work with that teacher again?" Madison asked. She was testing the idea the way she tested a hypothesis in science class, pushing on it to see if it held. "Would you trust anything they said afterward?"

"No way." Brennan paused. "Wait. So the treaty blamed Germany alone, and the whole country felt like..."

"Like you just did. Except a hundred times bigger." Madison scribbled fast, then crossed out a line and rewrote it. "That's the hidden part. You can't see resentment in a photograph. But it's there, and it's a factor in what came next."

Amari appeared from the WWI room, chewing the last of a granola bar. "Those cafe things are actually nutritious, unlike the vending machine. What'd I miss?"

"Madison figured out our whole presentation," Brennan said.

"Not the whole thing." Madison showed them her page. Three arrows ran from the treaty to the anger to the later war, and beside Article 231 she had written her group-project comparison. "When we present, I'll cite the article by number, and then I'll tell the class the project story. Mr. Nakamura said evidence plus a good analogy."

Amari read the page and nodded. "You should open with the blame part. Start small, then zoom out to the country."

The chime for regrouping sounded down the hall. Madison closed her notebook, hugged it against her chest, and headed for the doors with her two friends flanking her.

"First line," Amari said. "Say it to us like we're the class."

Madison took a breath. "Raise your hand if you've ever been blamed for something a whole group did."
